source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77

coverage.included: B.2.b — Prejudgment Remedies, attachment, injunction, Grupo Mexicano
coverage.note: No print-page labels present in ebook extraction; casebook problem statements are preserved as unsolved descriptions.

topics.title: B.2.b.i–iv — Prejudgment Attachment, Garnishment, Replevin and Due Process
topics.description: Provisional security before liability established, federal procedural due process, state requirements, ex parte judicial oversight, lien relation-back and creditor risks.

entries.title: Why provisional remedies are disfavored
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Prejudgment remedies preserve assets while litigation pending but burden defendant before creditor proves debt; usually require narrow statutory ground, due-process safeguards and bond.
entries.laymanExplanation: Freezing someone's property before they lose their lawsuit is a powerful weapon, so courts demand safeguards.
entries.legalExplanation: State prejudgment law generally governs; FRCP 64 makes forum-state seizure remedies available in federal court; avoid substituting ordinary postjudgment standard.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish pending suit vs final judgment; classify remedy and source.
entries.examTrap: An unsecured plaintiff cannot routinely seize assets just because it expects to win.

entries.title: Attachment vs garnishment vs replevin vs lis pendens
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Attachment seizes defendant's own nonexempt goods via sheriff; garnishment reaches defendant's property with third party; replevin recovers particular collateral based on asserted superior property right; lis pendens clouds title to disputed real estate.
entries.laymanExplanation: Attach pig, garnish bank account, replevy the lender's car, or warn land buyers litigation is pending.
entries.legalExplanation: An attachment/garnishment can be ancillary money remedy; replevin may stand alone when property right claimed; receiver and injunction are additional options.
entries.examApplication: Use who possesses property and creditor's preexisting lien to choose procedure.
entries.examTrap: Prejudgment garnishment subject to stricter safeguards than postjudgment garnishment.

entries.title: Supreme Court due-process cases restrict secret seizure
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Sniadach, Fuentes, Mitchell, North Georgia Finishing and Doehr assess constitutional fairness of withholding property before notice/hearing; not all ex parte remedies categorically unconstitutional.
entries.laymanExplanation: A judge can sometimes freeze assets without warning to prevent hiding, but the debtor must have meaningful procedural protection.
entries.legalExplanation: Procedures weigh creditor urgency, neutral judicial assessment, sworn facts, bond and prompt opportunity to challenge; casebook's summary emphasizes fair balance not universal pre-notice requirement.
entries.examApplication: If lawyer seeks ex parte relief evaluate whether judicial decision and evidence replace clerk rubber stamp.
entries.examTrap: Do not say Fuentes mandates prior adversary hearing for every provisional remedy.

entries.title: Five attachment procedural steps
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: (1) Creditor sues then files fact-based affidavit and bond; (2) judge evaluates likelihood of success plus statutory ground at ex parte hearing; (3) writ to sheriff; (4) sheriff levies and creates inchoate attachment lien; (5) debtor may substitute bond or seek quash; if creditor prevails lien matures/relates back.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sue, show why emergency freeze justified, secure a bond, judge issues writ, sheriff holds property, debtor can contest.
entries.legalExplanation: Common grounds imminent dissipation and nonresidency; strict statutory compliance is important.
entries.examApplication: Use chronological chart including filing, issuance, sheriff levy, intervening purchase and final judgment.
entries.examTrap: Merely signing affidavit is not the levy that gives lien priority.

entries.title: Attachment affidavit and creditor's bond
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Creditor usually must set forth concrete facts showing likely winning and statutory danger; bond secures debtor for damages if seizure wrong.
entries.laymanExplanation: You need evidence debtor may move assets away, not just say 'they're untrustworthy.'
entries.legalExplanation: Statutes typically require judge to assess support in ex parte hearing and creditor to post security against wrongful seizure.
entries.examApplication: Spot false/conclusory claims and missing bond.
entries.examTrap: Probable cause of honest collection may not defeat liability for wrongful attachment.

entries.title: Inchoate attachment lien and relation back
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Levy before judgment establishes conditional lien; if creditor wins final judgment, lien becomes choate and priority dates from prejudgment levy. If lawsuit dismissed, lien dissolves.
entries.laymanExplanation: Seizing Porky before trial reserves your spot if you eventually win; if you lose, spot vanishes.
entries.legalExplanation: Intervening purchasers and junior encumbrancers may take subject to earlier provisional lien.
entries.examApplication: For problems 1.15–1.17 compare March 3 levy, April sale and June judgment.
entries.examTrap: A writ merely issued to sheriff is not enough if no levy.

entries.title: Debtor motion to quash and bond substitution
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Debtor may move to vacate flawed provisional seizure for weak merits or statutory/procedural defect, may substitute bond for property; wrongful attachment damages possible.
entries.laymanExplanation: Debtor can recover use of property by posting security or showing freeze unauthorized.
entries.legalExplanation: Judicial oversight and prompt opportunity to contest serve due process; creditor assumes liability risk.
entries.examApplication: Analyze possibility of debtor prevailing or creditor voluntarily dismissing.
entries.examTrap: Good intentions do not validate unauthorized writ.

entries.title: Bankruptcy may undo recent prepetition provisional lien
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Casebook describes a 90-day avoidance risk under §547 if attachment/garnishment created shortly before filing, returning creditor to unsecured status when statutory preference elements met.
entries.laymanExplanation: The head start you got by grabbing property just before bankruptcy may be taken back.
entries.legalExplanation: Preference avoidance is element-driven and dates can matter; automatic consequence not appropriate without §547 elements; current book discussion previews later chapter.
entries.examApplication: Flag possible trustee preference lawsuit and avoid premature categorical result.
entries.examTrap: The 90-day window alone is not sufficient to conclude automatic avoidance.

entries.title: Strategic benefits and risks
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Prejudgment seizure secures claim, priority and leverage, but imposes costs, bond, liability risk and may provoke bankruptcy or later preference avoidance.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may freeze property but could end up paying damages or losing lien in bankruptcy.
entries.legalExplanation: Ask whether asset dissipation danger justifies expensive interim fight and whether state statutes support relief.
entries.examApplication: Offer both creditor and debtor perspectives in issue spotter.

topics.title: B.2.b.v — General-Creditor Asset-Freezes and Grupo Mexicano
topics.description: Full Supreme Court majority and Ginsburg dissent; law vs equity, FRCP 64/65, Mareva freezes and distinction from bankruptcy.

entries.title: General unsecured claimant usually has no property lien before judgment
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Without a property/security interest or judgment, general creditor usually lacks the vested interest in debtor's assets needed for broad traditional equitable asset-freeze.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if debtor owes you, you do not own its unencumbered bank account.
entries.legalExplanation: Traditional creditor's bill required prior judgment, and FRCP 65 cannot silently supply new substantive right; state attachment process may be available through Rule 64.
entries.examApplication: Ask if claim merely damages, or seeks specific equitable asset/trust/property.
entries.examTrap: Exception fact patterns involving existing lien, equitable claims or authorized statute require separate analysis.

entries.title: Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc., 527 U.S. 308 (1999)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: No. Federal equity under general authority did not historically permit such provisional asset-freeze for general nonjudgment creditor; Supreme Court reversed despite serious dissipation danger and likely meritorious claim.
entries.laymanExplanation: In ordinary pre-judgment money-damages case with no lien/equitable property claim, federal court lacks general inherent equity power to restrain disposition of debtor assets solely to assure future judgment.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Scalia majority confined federal equity to historically recognized substantive boundaries; a general creditor lacks property interest before judgment. FRCP 65 does not expand substantive rights, and broad freezes would bypass Rule 64's forum-state remedies and reshape delicate debtor-creditor priorities by judicial fiat. Post-1975 English Mareva practice not historical U.S. equity power. Ginsburg dissent emphasized flexible evolving equity, strong merits, irreparable injury, bond and preserving status quo without granting priority; Congress could regulate.
entries.examApplication: Analyze Rule 64 state remedies versus Rule 65 federal injunction and why bankruptcy/fraudulent transfer legislation addresses group creditor issues.
entries.examTrap: Decision does not forbid every injunction involving assets or all equitable claims, and majority did not dispute district court's factual concern.
entries.sourceRole: Excerpted opinion, majority and dissent, in Chapter 1
entries.facts: Mexican toll-road holding company defaulted on unsecured notes, faced insolvency and planned to favor Mexican creditors with sole remaining Toll Road Notes. Unsecured bondholders sued for $80.9m damages and won preliminary injunction freezing notes pending trial. District court found near-certain success and irreparable collection injury; Second Circuit upheld.
entries.issue: May federal district court in ordinary contract damages suit freeze unencumbered assets before judgment to secure potential money judgment when plaintiffs have no lien or equitable interest in assets?
entries.holding: No. Federal equity under general authority did not historically permit such provisional asset-freeze for general nonjudgment creditor; Supreme Court reversed despite serious dissipation danger and likely meritorious claim.
entries.reasoning: Justice Scalia majority confined federal equity to historically recognized substantive boundaries; a general creditor lacks property interest before judgment. FRCP 65 does not expand substantive rights, and broad freezes would bypass Rule 64's forum-state remedies and reshape delicate debtor-creditor priorities by judicial fiat. Post-1975 English Mareva practice not historical U.S. equity power. Ginsburg dissent emphasized flexible evolving equity, strong merits, irreparable injury, bond and preserving status quo without granting priority; Congress could regulate.
entries.rule: In ordinary pre-judgment money-damages case with no lien/equitable property claim, federal court lacks general inherent equity power to restrain disposition of debtor assets solely to assure future judgment.

entries.title: Mareva injunction contrasted with Grupo
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: English Mareva asset-freeze introduced in 1975 could stop dissipation pending action, but majority refused import into inherent historical American federal equity.
entries.laymanExplanation: England permits certain emergency freezes; the Supreme Court would not let federal judges invent same broad tool for ordinary unsecured contract plaintiffs.
entries.legalExplanation: U.S. Congress or applicable statutory/state process may provide alternatives; FRCP 64 channels ordinary state provisional remedies.
entries.examApplication: Compare Rule 64 (forum state remedies) and Rule 65 (federal injunction procedure).
entries.examTrap: The fact that equity merged with law procedurally did not enlarge creditors' substantive property rights.

entries.title: Ginsburg dissent: evolving equity and modern mobility of assets
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Dissent would affirm carefully tailored freeze with compelling proof, bond and little interference with operations because modern assets move fast and paper judgment may be worthless.
entries.laymanExplanation: A fair judgment is hollow if defendant can wire all assets away before trial.
entries.legalExplanation: Dissent contrasts dynamic conception of equity, irreparable harm and no priority creation with majority historical boundaries.
entries.examApplication: Explain why plaintiff's proposed restraint wasn't a perfected security interest.
entries.examTrap: Policy argument is dissent, not binding authority.

entries.title: Equity, bankruptcy and collective-creditor implications
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: A broad pre-judgment freezing tool might encourage a race of individual creditors and disrupt statutory bankruptcy, preferences and fraudulent transfer mechanisms.
entries.laymanExplanation: If everyone rushes to get injunctions, the failing business could collapse and other creditors suffer.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority treated systemic allocation choices as for Congress, not federal judges through generic equitable discretion.
entries.examApplication: Tie Grupo to central problem of protecting collective creditor pool.
entries.examTrap: A ban on ad hoc injunction doesn't make statutory bankruptcy impossible.

problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.2.b.i–iv — Prejudgment Attachment, Garnishment, Replevin and Due Process)
problems.prompt: Creditor sues Feb 1, writ obtained March 1, sheriff levies Porky March 3, debtor sells pig April 10, judgment June 1. Compare provisional relation-back and purchaser priority. Unsolved.

problems.title: Problem 1.17
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Chapter 1, § B.2.b; Effross Fall 2026 general syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.2.b.i–iv — Prejudgment Attachment, Garnishment, Replevin and Due Process)
problems.prompt: Creditor A attaches $20k art collection May 17 and gets $5k August judgment; Creditor Z already holds perfected $18k Article 9 lien since previous year. Analyze priorities and available collateral equity without solving.
